2.text: In still another story, Eᵋleˊnnut is described with the following details.

3.text: “Eᵋleˊnnut has long arms: they hang down lower than the knee. His fists

4.text: are like large round bowls made of the excrescences of a larch-tree. His

5.text: hands are stronger than iron. Eᵋleˊnnut is higher by a head than all other

6.text: people. His shoulders loom up in the middle of a throng, visible from afar,

7.text: like the shoulders of the wild reindeer-buck in a Chukchee reindeer-herd. He

8.text: runs in bounds over the deep snow, throwing up his legs. His track over

9.text: the snow is not double, but forms only one line. He eats with great haste,

10.text: gulping down piece after piece. All food is slippery for his throat. After

11.text: battle he is found in the sleeping-room. He is lying there with a young

12.text: woman. His legs are protruding from under the front part of the cover of

13.text: the room. Only the trembling of his hind part is to be seen.” Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn,

14.text: the Clamoring-One, is described as springing forward and clamoring for battle.

15.text: To the same group of warriors belongs young Čɪˊmkɪl. He is of modest

16.text: disposition. “There are four strong men,” says the story, — “Head-Nodder,

17.text: Eᵋleˊnnut, Aiñaˊɪrg̣ɪn, and Čɪˊmkɪl. In front of Čɪˊmkɪl sits his father. The

18.text: strong man silently waits till the old man speaks his words.”

19.text: Of other warriors should be mentioned Nankačhaˊt, — “a big, heavy

20.text: man, clad throughout in the hide of a thong-seal. The head of his spear is

21.text: a cubit long. In the time of drifting ice on the Omvaˊan River, he lies down

22.text: across the river and stops the ice. The drifting floes are stopped, his body

23.text: forms a bridge, and the caravans of reindeer-sledges pass over him as on

24.text: firm ground.” These exaggerated details surpass the usual style of Chukchee

26.text: In another tale he drives his spear into the bottom of the river. The

27.text: moving ice is stopped. The ice forms a temporary bridge, over which pass

28.text: the Chukchee caravans. The latter version comes nearer to the usual style

30.text: In still another tale appears the strong man Aᵋttɪmlu or Aᵋmluᵋ, which

31.text: means “bony face.” He is called so because his face is quite hard. The

32.text: arrows of the Taˊn˙ñɪt cannot hurt it. Eᵋleˊnnut lives with him as a companion

34.text: “Bony-Face quarrelled with Head-Nodder, and slapped him on the head with his open hand.

35.text: From this slap the other suffered throughout the summer. After that the offended one wanted to

36.text: have revenge. He exercised for two consecutive years, in order to equal Bony-Face in strength.

37.text: Then he called his brother and went to visit the offender. His brother’s name was Yɪrkɪtowaˊʟaᵋn;

38.text: i.e., ‘having soft buttocks.’ Bony-Face proposed to pay them for the offence; first two thong-seal

39.text: skins, then two beaver-skins; but they refused. Then all four went out of the house. Eᵋleˊnnut

40.text: sat down upon a sledge as an onlooker. Bony-Face turned up his sleeves. The two adversaries

41.text: caught him from both sides. ‘What! both of you?’ — ‘Yes, both of us.’ — ‘Ah, all right!’ He

42.text: caught them both by the nape of the neck and pushed them together face to face, then threw

43.text: them upon the ground. The snow was covered with blood, as from a reindeer newly slaughtered.

44.text: Then he turned away and entered his house again.”
